notes: Step 1 parts were correct and are unchanged.

The manual shows three diagrams. I built the two-button breadboard diagram with a common ground rail, because it is the only one that uses a breadboard. It also contains the GPIO 17 single-button circuit.

Pin mapping on the Pi's 40-pin header, read from the diagram: GND is physical pin 6 (row GP3/GND), GPIO17 is pin 11, GPIO5 is pin 29. The Pi is modelled as raspberry-pi-4-gpio, which uses physical pin numbers.

Each button straddles the centre gap in columns e and f. Button 1 spans rows 5 and 7, and button 2 spans rows 10 and 12. Side 1 (1.l/1.r) is the upper row, which goes to ground. Side 2 (2.l/2.r) is the lower row, which goes to the GPIO pin. Pressing a button joins the two sides.

The negative rail is the left rail in the diagram. It is modelled as the single top-negative strip 'tn', with wire ends at tn.1, tn.5 and tn.10. In the picture this rail is drawn with a small gap partway down. I treated it as one continuous strip, since the diagram highlights the whole run in black.
No resistors are used. The buttons connect the GPIO pin to ground when pressed, so they rely on the Pi's internal pull-up resistors, as the manual implies.
